Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Maladaptive Strategies.value: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, military/police uniforms are not a plausible primary trigger unless there is additional trauma context; this item points to an interpersonal/authority-related trauma theme not represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Triggers: Name Reminders: Hearing related names
issues.explanation: 'Hearing related names' is hard to reconcile with natural disaster as the index trauma unless a specific deceased/injured person is central, which is not supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for someone entering the home implies an interpersonal intruder/assailant threat rather than disaster-related danger, creating a cross-node mismatch with the trauma type and trigger/memory content.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: Feeling safe only in a very limited number of places can occur in PTSD, but here it clusters with home-intruder monitoring and touch avoidance into an interpersonal-danger profile that is poorly matched to natural disaster trauma.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat item implies fear of an intruder or interpersonal attack in the home, which is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma profile. With flooding/water triggers present, the expected threat would be environmental danger rather than someone entering the home.

issues.item: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but here it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no negative-appraisal items about personal blame, humiliation, or moral failure that would make shame a coherent central memory response.

issues.item: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Avoiding all physical contact is more characteristic of interpersonal trauma and is not clinically well linked to the reported disaster-related triggers and memory items. It addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in the profile.

vignette:
Marisol Herrera is a 57-year-old physical therapist who came to treatment more than a year after surviving a catastrophic flood. Divorced and living alone, she had built a steady life around work, routine, and a strong sense of competence. Before the disaster, she thought of herself as practical and calm under pressure, the kind of clinician who could steady frightened patients with her voice and hands. The event that now returns to her began during a period of heavy rain when water rose through her neighborhood with a speed she still struggles to describe. She remembers standing inside her home and seeing water where it should never have been, pushing under the door and then climbing higher, carrying debris and a force that made ordinary rooms feel suddenly unreal. At some point names shouted outside-the street name, neighbors' names, the name of the river repeated by emergency responders and people trying to find one another-became fused with panic. What remains most potent for her now is anything that evokes that scene: the sight of floodwater on the news, a large body of water she happens to pass, or even hearing certain names linked in her mind to that day.

In the weeks after, Marisol found that the memory would not come back in an orderly way. At times it felt as if it had happened to somebody else, as though she were describing a film she had seen rather than her own life. At other times she was overtaken by the full force of terror and sorrow without any clear picture at all. She would be sitting quietly and suddenly feel the same surge in her body-her stomach turning, her chest tightening, grief crashing over her-without an image she could point to. When she does deliberately try to recall the flood, what comes most strongly is overwhelming grief. She does not elaborate it into dramatic language; instead she goes quiet, looks down, and says that remembering leaves her feeling hollowed out.

Marisol has become highly attentive to signs that something bad could happen again. Unexpected or loud sounds make her jolt immediately alert. A crash in the apartment building, a slammed car door outside, even a sudden clatter at the clinic can leave her heart racing before she has had time to think. Nights have become especially difficult. She lies awake listening, feeling that she cannot fully relax, or wakes repeatedly and scans the room before she can settle again. Over time, safety has narrowed for her. She says she only feels safe in a very limited number of places, essentially her apartment and a few familiar rooms at work. Beyond those spaces, she feels exposed and tense.

Her work as a physical therapist brings these difficulties into daily view. She still goes to the clinic, but not with the same ease. If a patient mentions living near the river, or if she hears the name of an area associated in her mind with the flood, she feels nausea rise abruptly and has to focus on staying composed. Visual reminders are difficult too; a rehabilitation room television showing storm footage or even a conversation about waterfront property can leave her feeling unsteady. She has increasingly limited her life outside these controlled settings. She goes out less than she used to, turning down invitations and keeping errands brief and necessary. What seems sensible to her is staying where she can manage herself, where exits are known and the surroundings feel contained.

When distress peaks, Marisol tries to make herself go blank. She described deliberately attempting to leave her body, to become numb and absent until the feeling passes. In the moment this seems like the only way to get through the wave of nausea, dread, or grief, especially when there is no clear image attached to it. She also spends long stretches dwelling on who she was before the flood. She measures herself against that earlier version-more spontaneous, more willing to go anywhere, less guarded-and the comparison has become painful. The losses feel personal and daily rather than abstract: she no longer moves through the world with the same trust, and her life has contracted around a few safe places.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was exhausted by poor sleep and by the effort of holding herself together at work. What finally pushed her to come in was the realization that her world had become so small that even an ordinary day could feel like an ordeal if it included the wrong sound, the wrong name, or the sight of water. She said she is frightened that this is simply who she is now, someone who can never fully come back into her own life. At the same time, she still hopes she might regain some part of the woman she remembers being before the flood, and be able to leave home, work, and rest without bracing for the next wave.
